key_insight: Pretraining on a large source PDE dataset can significantly improve data efficiency when adapting to a new geometry, but the gain depends on what kind of distribution shift is present. The paper shows that changes in geometry and changes in modeled physics do not help or hurt pretraining in the same way.
problem_solved: The paper addresses a key uncertainty in neural PDE surrogates: which components of distribution shift—such as geometry changes versus physics/model changes—determine how much benefit pretraining provides during fine-tuning.
method: Pretrained a neural PDE surrogate on 254,909 RANS simulations from one airfoil family.

Fine-tuned the model on a different airfoil family under two target settings with matched freestream ranges: one with the same Spalart-Allmaras (SA) turbulence model and one with SA plus e^N transition modeling.
Compared pretrained vs. non-pretrained adaptation to isolate how geometry shift and physics shift affect data efficiency.
Evaluated performance at a fixed training budget (N=1000) to measure the practical value of pretraining.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners building surrogate models for CFD and scientific computing, this study clarifies when pretraining is most valuable and when its benefits may be limited by distribution shift. It can help guide data collection, transfer learning strategy, and model deployment across new engineering conditions.
visual_elements: Two-stage pipeline diagram: source pretraining on one airfoil family → fine-tuning on a new family
Side-by-side comparison panels for the two target settings: SA vs. SA + e^N transition
Bar chart showing data efficiency or error reduction with and without pretraining at N=1000
Icon-based summary of shift types: geometry shift, physics shift, freestream-matched conditions
paper_title: How Does Distribution Shift Shape Pretraining Gains in Neural PDE Surrogates?
paper_authors: Pochinapeddi Sai Bhargav, Nithin Somasekharan, Rohit Sunil Kanchi, Sicheng He, Shaowu Pan
